id: Body of Rags, International Bridge Between the US & Mexico

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Is it alive? —neither a head, legs nor arms! ................... ... torpid against the flange of the supporting girder . ? an inhuman shapelessness, knees hugged tight up into the belly Egg-shaped! —William Carlos Williams, 1950 visit to El Paso, from “Desert Music” Yes, I am a body of rags lying here on the bridge waiting for a hot rain to wash me open, dissolve me off the bridge because this border is closed. I rot on the boundary line and can’t enter Juarez, pennies thrown at me when a drunk El Pasoan returns in the darkness and sees my shape that makes him hurry across. No head, decades ago they threw it in the river without my screams. My arms were the first to go when I couldn’t climb the wall. I can never leave this bridge. I live on the pure line that divides countries and grabs my hunger from sliding into Mexico with my outstretched hands. I still have my knees. I used to be sold in Juarez and smuggled into El Paso, the egg that floated down the Rio Grande to break hundreds of miles away before being thrown back. I stay on the bridge and can’t move. Do not cross to El Paso without wiping your shoes of me, one foot on US concrete, the other scraping away at my Mexican rags. When I struggle against the wire fence, I make sure I salute two flags.

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version that refines the flow and language while preserving the original imagery, structure, and meaning:

---

*Is it alive? —neither a head, nor legs, nor arms!*
*...................*
*... torpid against the flange of the supporting girder .*
*? an inhuman shapelessness,*
*knees hugged tight up into the belly*
*Egg-shaped!*

—William Carlos Williams, from "Desert Music," recounting his 1950 visit to El Paso

Yes, I am a body of rags, lying here upon the bridge,
waiting for a scalding rain to wash me open,
to dissolve me from this bridge—
for this border is closed.
I rot along the boundary line,
unable to enter Juárez,
pennies flung at me
when a drunken El Pasoan returns through the darkness
and, seeing my shape, quickens his step across.

No head—decades ago they cast it into the river,
without waiting for my screams.
My arms were the first to go,
when I could no longer scale the wall.
I can never leave this bridge.
I live upon the pure line that divides nations
and holds my hunger back
from sliding into Mexico
with my outstretched hands.

I still have my knees.
Once, I was sold in Juárez and smuggled into El Paso—
the egg that drifted down the Rio Grande
to break hundreds of miles away
before being thrown back.
I remain upon the bridge and cannot move.

Do not cross into El Paso
without first wiping your shoes of me—
one foot upon the concrete of the States,
the other scraping away my Mexican rags.
And when I strain against the wire fence,
I take care to salute both flags.

---

Would you like me to offer a version that stays even closer to the original wording, or one that leans further into formal, literary polish?
outputs.L2:
**Epigraph (from William Carlos Williams, 1950, during a trip to El Paso, "Desert Music"):**

Can it be living? —there's no head, no legs, no arms visible! ................... ... slumped and motionless upon the ridge of the beam that holds up the structure . ? a formlessness that seems less than human, with knees drawn up firmly against the stomach Shaped like an egg! 

---

Indeed, I'm nothing but a heap of tattered cloth stretched out across this bridge, hoping for a warm downpour to break me apart, to melt me away from these boards, since the crossing has been sealed. I decay along the dividing line, unable to pass into Juarez. Coins get tossed my way whenever some intoxicated man from El Paso stumbles home through the night and spots my outline, which sends him rushing past. I have no head—years back they hurled it into the water, and I never cried out. My arms disappeared first, back when I failed to scale the barrier. This bridge will hold me forever. I dwell upon that sharp boundary separating nations, the line that keeps my starving, reaching hands from slipping down toward Mexico. My knees remain with me still. Once, I was for sale in Juarez, then trafficked over into El Paso—the egg that drifted along the Rio Grande only to shatter miles and miles downstream before being tossed back again. I remain fixed on this bridge, incapable of movement. Don't step across into El Paso without scraping me off your shoes—one foot planted on American pavement, the other rubbing away my Mexican tatters. And as I strain and fight against the barbed fencing, I always take care to honor both flags at once.
outputs.L3:
# The Border Body: An Analysis

The poem gives voice to a dehumanized, dismembered figure—reduced to "a body of rags"—that lies trapped on the bridge separating El Paso from Juárez. Through this haunting persona, the poet transforms an abstract political boundary into a visceral, embodied experience of suffering and abandonment. The speaker is not merely a witness to border violence but has become its very embodiment, a discarded thing left to languish in the liminal space between two nations.

Central to the poem's power is the speaker's paralysis. Unable to move in either direction, the figure exists permanently on the boundary line that divides the two countries, denied passage into both Mexico and the United States. This immobility captures the cruel limbo experienced by so many migrants—caught between a homeland they cannot return to and a destination that refuses to receive them. The bridge, ordinarily a symbol of connection and transit, becomes instead a site of eternal suspension.

The figure's physical mutilation serves as a potent symbol of the border's violence. Having lost its head to the river and its arms while attempting to climb the wall, the body bears the literal marks of the dangers migrants face. These are not abstract wounds but specific injuries tied to the mechanisms of border enforcement and the natural barriers that claim so many lives. The dismemberment renders visible the human cost that official statistics and political rhetoric so often obscure.

This sense of futility deepens through the imagery of the egg, smuggled and floated down the Rio Grande. The image evokes the cyclical, seemingly hopeless journey of migrants who, despite their efforts, are broken and "thrown back." The fragility of the egg underscores the vulnerability of those who undertake such crossings, while its circular journey suggests a pattern of repeated attempts and repeated failures—a Sisyphean ordeal with no promise of resolution.

Finally, the poem confronts the profound dehumanization of border crossers directly. From the pennies thrown by drunk passersby to the travelers who scrape the speaker's "Mexican rags" off their shoes, the figure is treated not as a human being but as refuse—an object of casual contempt and careless cruelty. These small, degrading gestures accumulate into a devastating indictment of how migrants are perceived and treated. In giving voice to this silenced, broken body, the poem demands that readers recognize the humanity that such treatment seeks to erase.

# Reclaiming the Shapeless Figure: A Response to Williams

In his writings, William Carlos Williams once described a figure he encountered at the El Paso–Juárez border in terms that stripped it of humanity—a shapeless, egg-like form that seemed to lack the defining features of a person. This poem emerges as a direct and deliberate response to that dehumanizing portrayal. Rather than allowing the figure to remain a passive object of another's gaze, the poem reclaims it, granting it a voice and a first-person perspective that Williams's original description denied. In doing so, the poem overturns the power dynamic inherent in the act of observation, insisting that the observed possesses an interiority, a consciousness, and a story of its own.

The poem accomplishes this transformation through vivid and unflinching imagery. It depicts a body that is mutilated and immobile, trapped upon the bridge that divides the United States and Mexico. This bridge, a physical structure spanning the border, becomes a charged symbol of suspension and liminality—a place where the migrant is caught between two nations, belonging fully to neither. The immobility of the figure speaks to the paralysis and helplessness experienced by those who find themselves stranded at the threshold of a hoped-for future, while the mutilation of the body evokes both literal violence and the deeper wounds inflicted by systems of exclusion and indifference.

Through these images, the poem powerfully conveys the profound physical and existential suffering endured by border migrants. The pain is at once bodily and spiritual: the aching, broken flesh mirrors an interior anguish born of displacement, rejection, and the constant threat of erasure. Yet the poem does not leave its subject in a state of pure degradation. Instead, it performs a crucial act of transformation, taking what Williams rendered as a symbol of formlessness and worthlessness and reshaping it into a poignant assertion of dignity and identity. By speaking as the figure rather than about it, the poem restores humanity to the dehumanized, affirming the enduring selfhood of those whom borders and prejudices would render invisible.

# The Perfect Breakfast

William had always prided himself on making the perfect breakfast, and the centerpiece of his morning ritual was always the humble **egg**. Whether scrambled, poached, or sunny-side up, he believed that a well-cooked egg could set the tone for the entire day.

One Saturday morning, his neighbor **Carlos** knocked on the door, drawn by the irresistible aroma drifting through the open kitchen window.

"William, you have to teach me your secret," Carlos said with a grin. "My eggs always turn out rubbery."

William chuckled and waved him inside. "The trick is patience," he explained, cracking a fresh **egg** into a warm, buttered pan. "Low heat, and never rush it."

Carlos watched intently as the edges gently set, the yolk still glistening and soft in the center. William slid the finished dish onto a plate and handed it over.

"Try this," he said.

Carlos took a bite and his eyes widened. "This is incredible! I never knew a simple **egg** could taste so good."

From that day forward, the two neighbors met every weekend to cook breakfast together. What started as a lesson about eggs slowly grew into a genuine friendship, proving that sometimes the simplest things—a good meal and good company—are the ones worth savoring most.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem responding to William Carlos Williams' description of the "shapeless" figure on the bridge in "Desert Music," told from the perspective of that figure stuck on the El Paso–Juárez border.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Shapeless Thing Remembers**

You called me *shapeless*, poet,
as if a body were a promise
the wind had failed to keep.
But I am the shape the bridge makes
when it forgets which country
it is holding up.

Beneath me the Rio runs its thin argument,
a thread the two cities pull
until the seam splits and neither
will claim the fallen button.
That is where you found me—
propped, you said, *motionless*,
a bundle the color of nothing
you had a word for.

I heard you pass. I heard the music
you kept naming like a man
convincing himself the desert sings.
It does. It sings in the register
of the ones who cannot cross,
a note so low you take it
for the traffic, for your own
breathing, for the hum
inside the concrete.

I am not your riddle.
I am the pause the guards step over,
the punctuation between two flags.
El Paso at my back like a stove
gone cold, Juárez ahead
holding out its hands of dust.
I belong to the middle,
the un-nation, the exact width
of a line drawn by men
who never had to sit on it.

You wanted to make a poem of me,
to prove the imagination
survives even here—
and it does. Look:
I have imagined a country
where a body is not shapeless
but simply *tired*, simply
folded like a letter
no one will deliver,
addressed in a language
the river keeps trying to read
aloud.

So walk on, poet.
Take your music home.
Leave me the shape you couldn't name.
I'll wear it through the night
like the only coat
that fits a man
who is from both sides
and welcome
on neither.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a persona poem in the voice of a body of rags lying on the international bridge between El Paso and Juárez, using the William Carlos Williams epigraph about the egg-shaped figure. Explore themes of borders, immigration, and dehumanization.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Bridge Holds

*"so much depends / upon"*
—after William Carlos Williams

---

I am the shape they step around,
egg-curled against the concrete seam
where one nation's paint stops
and another's begins—

so much depends
upon this body
of rags, this heap
that used to answer

to a name. I have become
a landmark now, a thing
the tourists photograph
from the safe height of their walking,

a smudge the color of nothing,
of dust, of the river
they say is a border
though water knows no such word.

*So much depends.*

I lie in the exact middle,
belonging to neither foot
that hurries past—too *here*
for one flag, too *there* for the other,

I am the hyphen
they cannot pronounce,
the dash between two countries
that means *stop* and means *wait*

and means *you were almost*.
Beneath me the current pulls
its old argument south,
carrying what the desert refused.

I remember being vertical.
I remember hands
that were mine, that reached,
that filled out forms in a language

of stamps and denials.
Now I am horizontal grammar,
a sentence laid down,
a period the crowds walk over

thinking: *not my country,
not my problem, not
a person, only
what a person leaves behind.*

So much depends
upon the pretending—
that a body is a bundle,
that rags were never warm,

that the wind through my sleeves
is only wind
and not the last
thing I am trying to say.

Above me: two flags.
Below me: one river.
Around me: the great
indifferent commerce of legs.

I am the still point
the whole bridge balances on,
the weight they will not lift,
the question mark

curled at the border's foot—
*so much depends,*
*so much,*
*upon.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Using this quote from Williams' "Desert Music" as an epigraph, write a border poem where the figure without a head or arms speaks for itself: "Is it alive? —neither a head, legs nor arms!"
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Body Says

I am the shape the river left,
the thing that crossed and did not finish crossing.
You ask if I am living
because I have no mouth to answer,
yet here—listen—the wind
plays my hollow like a flute.

They found me at the seam of two countries,
neither a head, legs nor arms,
just the trunk of a question
half-buried in the sand.

I was a man once, or a woman,
or the idea of a passage—
the swollen middle of a journey
where the heart is kept.

Do not mistake my silence for surrender.
I am the torso of everyone
who folded themselves small enough
to fit through wire, through night,
through the eye of the border's needle.

My arms? I gave them to the crossing,
reaching for the far bank.
My legs? They walked until they became the walking.
My head? It thought too much of home
and stayed behind to keep the fire.

What remains is the essential drum,
the container that carried breath,
the vessel the desert could not empty
though it tried, though it tries still,
sanding me down to this—

a body that is only body,
alive in the way a stone is alive
when it holds the day's heat
long after the sun has gone,
warm to the hand that finally,
finally, reaches for it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about the US-Mexico border in which the speaker is a broken, dismembered figure trapped on the dividing line, unable to enter either country. Begin with an epigraph from William Carlos Williams.
counterfactuals.output:
*The pure products of America / go crazy—*
—William Carlos Williams

I am the seam no thread will close,
laid out along a line drawn once in ink
and now in rust, in wire, in the long
arithmetic of dust.

They took my right hand
and buried it in Sonora
where it still opens and closes
around a fistful of someone's name.

They took my left
and left it in Texas
under a courthouse floor,
palm up, asking.

My spine is the fence itself—
each vertebra a post,
each nerve a strand of barbed wire
singing when the wind
or the searchlight
touches it.

I cannot walk south:
my knees are pledged to the north.
I cannot walk north:
my feet are sworn to the south.
So I stand, if you can call it standing,
a scarecrow stitched from two flags
that will not agree
on the color of my blood.

The river runs through the hollow of me
and takes what it wants—
a shoe, a rosary, a boy's photograph
folded to the size of a promise.
I feel it pass like a swallow
through the empty barn of my chest.

At night the coyotes,
the real ones, the four-legged,
come to lick the salt
from my exposed ribs,
and I do not stop them.
We are all of us
trying to cross something.

My mouth is in one country,
my ear in another,
so every word I speak
arrives translated into silence
by the time it reaches me.

I have learned to be a threshold:
neither door nor wall,
only the cold jamb between,
the place where the wind
sits down to rest
and decides it belongs to no one.

Bury me, someone.
But you cannot—
half of me would rise in Ciudad Juárez,
half in El Paso,
and the two halves
would stand facing
across all that dividing dark,
each waving the other's severed hand,
neither able to say
come home,
come home,
come home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem that reimagines the shapeless bridge figure from Williams' 1950 visit to El Paso as a metaphor for undocumented migrants, incorporating imagery of the Rio Grande, the wire fence, and two flags.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Shape on the Bridge**

*after William Carlos Williams' "The Desert Music"*

There it was again—the formless form,
the thing that is neither entering nor leaving,
slumped at the seam of two countries
like a question no map will answer.

Williams saw it in 1950 and could not name it,
a lump against the railing, a body
made of waiting, of nowhere,
the color of the dust the wind rehearses.

Now I give it a name it never chose:
*migrant*, *the undocumented*, *the shapeless*,
the human comma between two clauses of nation,
holding the whole sentence still.

Below, the Rio Grande does what water does—
refuses the line we drew across it,
carries silt from one flag to the other
without a stamp, without a fee,

the river a document no one can revoke,
older than the border it dissolves,
brown and shallow and utterly free
to be what we are forbidden to be.

And the fence—that wire that stitches nothing,
that ripped hem of the desert,
where a shirt has snagged and gone to thread,
where the light itself gets caught and torn—

it does not stop the shape.
The shape has become the fence's opposite:
soft where the wire is sharp,
patient where the steel keeps score.

Two flags snap above the checkpoint,
each certain it is the true sky.
The eagle on one, the eagle on the other,
both feeding on the same small figure between.

But the shape endures their argument.
It is not a citizen of either wind.
It is only itself, only breathing,
only the music the desert keeps hidden—

that thing that is, that dances even here,
huddled and heavy and impossibly alive,
proving what Williams half-suspected:
the poem, like the person, refuses to disappear.
